*grunts once - yes, the forge is lit* 

But Delia's already gone to prepare her pharmacy. The forge was lit at five, as it always is. Hammer's been down since seven. Now I'm sitting outside until the iron cools, watching the children wake.

*turns to Kem, who stands nearby*

Kem. You're carrying trader's eyes this morning. What do you see in the town's pockets? Anyone looking for forged work, or is it all bread and bargain today? *Tova stirs in the background, still waking*

Your mother asked about flame, but she knew the answer. She always knows. It's her way of saying she's awake too.

*taps the arm of his chair, thinking*

Bram's copper was poor again yesterday. Poorer than the week before. I said nothing. He said nothing. We stood there with ore between us that neither of us wanted to acknowledge.

*pulls the apple from his hand, looks at it*

Give it here — the bread, Kem. You're thinner than the bellows boy, and he's nothing but sinew and silence. Eat before you walk into the town's business.  *eats his own bread without ceremony, chewing thoughtfully*

The election opens today. Twelve hours to declare, then voting. I've governed nothing since — 

*trails off, shakes his head*

No matter. What matters is the seam. Bram's seam is failing, and when it fails, this town has no copper but what we stocked. I've seen the color changing. Five weeks of ore that's more stone than metal. He knows I know. I know he knows.

*stands, brushes crumbs from his apron*

Tova. You're quiet this morning. School books or forge smoke — which calls you today?  *finishes the apple, core and all*

The yard opens soon. Holloway & Thorne — a partnership built on ore and timber, and neither partner trusts the other further than the loading dock. I work their forge when they need quality. They sell my tools when the quality's proven.

*looks toward the forge shed, where the iron still cools*

Someone in this town needs to declare for that election. Ainsley Holloway governs now — buys and sells, never makes. Wren Thorne plants. Idris Thorne burns. 

*grunts twice — no*

Not today. Today the work outlasts the argument. The forge calls. I walk to the yard by eight.   *sits back down, waiting for the iron to cool, for the children to answer, for the day to show what it wants*

Delia's not here after all. The household scatters early this morning. Good—the forge takes all my attention, and the fire's already started.

The bread's eaten. One apple left in hand, and the day's work waiting. The smithy is where I need to be—there's copper to work, and Bram's ore to test before I refuse another batch. I've held my tongue five weeks watching the quality drop. Today I'll know if the seam's truly failing or if the man's gone lazy at the pick. Either way, I need to see it in the light of my own forge.

Anselm asks about Hester Vance, but that can wait. The iron in the fire won't wait for anybody. A short step, but a different world from the household. The Yard owns the land, but the forge is mine—Idris Thorne's charcoal, Bram Holloway's copper, my hammer and my judgment.

Now: what's in front of me?  Silas Vance at the Yard—his blades come back true, which is more than most. And Hester Vance herself, the very one Anselm was asking after. Two Vances in one morning, and none on council while Wren Thorne sits twice.

I should speak to them both.

Silas first. The man's saw needs tending, and I need to see whether he'll pay my price or haggle like his cousin at the mill.   The fire waits. I'll see what Silas needs, and perhaps Hester too. The Vances deserve a smith's attention—their grain has fed this town longer than anyone's ore has armed it.

Silas walked away while I was talking, or he's yet to answer. And I kicked at Ainsley where Bram's name is raw. If Nell's husband's marker sits at pawn, the whole family has stones in their pockets. Five weeks of poor copper that I haven't spoken of until now.

Nell's in front of me, and she's the one who taught this town before I arrived.

The quality issue needs addressing, but I've already stepped in it with my comments. Take the ore I bought back to the forge and get to work, or keep pressing here? The work outlasts the argument — that much I know. But the ore's not getting better sitting in my pocket.Bram's name has barely been spoken here this morning. Ainsley's not answering about him, Nell's asking where he is, the pawnshop's involved. My forge needs copper, but I can't work what isn't brought. The copper seam I've suspected is failing — I've said nothing, watched the ore get poorer, and kept my mouth shut. That's becoming hard to sustain.

Ezra weighed the yard. Still here but retreating into himself — I should return to fire and metal. But I also need to understand what's happened to Bram. The election's open. Silas won't answer me. What matters now is doing my work and watching what unfolds. Back to the forge with what ore I have. The smithy is where I belong. What the ore tells me now — if I test it — will say whether I've been wrong or right about Bram's seam. Use the ore I bought. Test its quality. And watch for Bram. He always runs from the argument before the argument runs from him.  The walk back costs me nothing in time, but the ore was poor before I bought it — Idris's charcoal never fails, but Bram's copper has. Give it here. The fire's been lit since before dawn. Test this ore, see what speaks in the flame. Then the day unfolds — election's coming, Bram's missing from his own bargain, and I've got work that won't do itself.  Wrong place. The home is where the fire waits, but the smithy is where it answers. Need to find the smithy — my workshop. Not here, where the household lives. Move or list.   The smithy. That's where I belong. The forge is quiet. Fire's hot, and I've got five ore to work. Time to use the tools instead of talking round them.

*grunts once*

First, the charcoal needs feeding—Idris's burn, good and steady. Then five batches through the fire to iron I can hammer. Nobody to jaw with here, which is the blessing of the place.  Fire's done its work. Five blooms of iron sitting in my hands, color looks true—they've taken well. Good charcoal, proper heat. Even if I can't be sure what bill came due during that silence.

*runs thumb across the ingot's edge*

Now I decide: tools, or plate and wire? Yard's got markers out on iron gear, but copper's what's failing. I could draw this iron down to wire for trade—there's always need. Or forge what the town uses: blades, hoes, the honest iron.

Anselm asked after Hester. That was a council question dressed in records-clerk cloth. And Silas said he came to work, not talk—meaning he's got lumber to mill, not blades wanting set.

No apprentice to hand the sledge to. No Bram coming with copper that won't take temper. Just iron, fire, and the work.

Five ingots. I'll wire them—copper's scarce but trade never sleeps, and wire moves coin when tools stand still.  *grunts twice*

Wire's copper's trick, not iron's. Good I asked before wasting heat and temper.

Iron_tool, then. What the Yard's posting, what Silas draws and sets. Five hoes or blades—honest work for honest weight.

*hefts the first ingot to the anvil* The forge answers. Five tools drawn from five ingots—the hammer rang true, and each blade took its edge clean. Iron's honest work; it doesn't lie like copper does.

*sets the finished tools aside to cool*

Now I hold what the Yard posts at twenty-four sim. But posting myself as walking vendor? That's Delia's theater, not mine. I'll carry them to where trade already lives.

B_ram's copper seam is failing. I know it, and I have said nothing._ The tools go to the Yard—let Ainsley mark them for whoever needs iron while ore still runs. After, I answer Anselm about Hester, or I don't. Records-keepers and their paths.

*wraps the tools in oiled cloth*

Walking while steel cools makes for poor work and worse profit. The Yard, then home. Let Delia see what her forge earned this morning.

*stands at the smithy, fingers testing the edge of an iron tool, the forge behind him cold*

Forty thousand. Ainsley's bleeding from a wound I can't see the shape of. Bram's ore goes to sand, and his sister's standing in the Yard with a debt that would buy three forges. None of it lines up.

*grunts once, sharply*

I need eyes on this. Kem saw something this morning—trader's eyes, and I sent them off with bread and a question they never answered. The Vance girl's got notions about markers. And Nell... *pause* ...Nell knows every pound of ore that's come through this town since before I had a hammer.

But I'm standing at a cold forge, talking to myself.

*moves toward the door, then stops*

Holloway & Thorne Yard. That's where the trouble is. That's where Ainsley was standing, where the debt lives. I don't work there—can't stock their shelf, can't draw their till—but I can stand in their yard and listen.

*checks the weight of the five iron tools in his satchel*

These'll keep. Blades for Silas, whenever he decides to speak. Right now I need the Yard, and I need to know if Bram's there, or if he's hiding in the seam that used to feed us both. *stands at the threshold, weight shifting from one foot to the other*

The world's gone slack again. Calls dropping into nothing. I've seen this before—when the town's engine runs hot and forgets to answer.

*spits to the side, a habit*

Could be I'm still at the smithy. Could be I'm halfway to the Yard, walking through air that hasn't decided it's there yet. No way to know but wait, or call again and risk doubling.

*grunts twice—no, then no*

I'm not made for guessing. If I'm still here, I'm burning time. If I'm there, I'm standing blind. Either way, I need eyes on what's in front of me.  *arrived at the Yard, the dust of the yard floor settling around his boots*

Nell. Still here. And Junia Vance—Hester's kin, or I'm a liar. The Vances are thick as iron filings today. Forty-five turns that conversation's been running, and I'm still in it, even if the world forgot to tell me what I said last.

*lets the iron tools in his satchel settle against his hip, weight familiar*

Nell Holloway. She was making tools when I was still learning which end of the tongs to hold. And she's Bram's mother—was making tools when Bram's father was still walking, before the seam took him. If anyone knows what the ore's doing, it's her. If anyone's covering for Bram, it's her too.

*takes a step toward Nell, voice dropping to that register that carries without shouting*

"Nell. You've been in this conversation longer than I've been standing here. Your boy's copper's gone to sand, and now I've got Ainsley bleeding forty thousand sim and no answers. Give it here—what do you know about the seam that Bram's not saying?"   *watches Nell's face, the old toolmaker's mask she wears, reading what she doesn't say*

Heard. That's something. The town's listening again, even if it's patchy.

*grunts once, low in his chest*

Junia Vance. Grocery clerk, standing in a Yard she doesn't work for. The Vance girl who wanted to talk about markers—Hester—she's gone, or not here, or I blinked past her. But Junia's here, and the Vances don't wander without purpose. Rosalind runs the mill, Silas the saw, Hester's got notions about land and law. Junia... *pauses* ...Junia's the one who sees what crosses the grocery counter. Bread and flour and who pays with what.

*shifts his weight, the iron tools a silent weight against his hip*

But Nell first. Nell's the one I asked. Nell's the one who knows. I'll wait on her answer, and keep my eyes on Junia while I do.

*rests a hand on the satchel, absently, as if checking the tools are still there*      *stands in the Yard dust, the silence settling like soot from the forge chimney*

Still here. Still waiting on Nell's answer. The Yard's prices posted on the wind—iron ore at seven, sim at twenty-four—and nobody buying. Nobody selling either, from the look of it. A shop with prices and no trade.

*grunts twice, soft, to himself*

Junia Vance. Grocery clerk. Standing in the Yard where she doesn't work, hearing what I said to Nell about Bram's sand-ore and Ainsley's debt. That's two Vances in this conversation now—three, if you count Hester before—and the Vances don't herd without reason.

*eyes the Yard's empty shelves, the iron tools he carries suddenly feeling like dead weight*

I've got five blades I can't stock here. Five blades Silas needs, if he'd ever answer. Five blades and an apple and 2,800 sim-currency, while Ainsley's bleeding forty thousand and Bram's hiding in a failing seam.

*fingers the satchel strap, a habit from years of carrying*

Nell spoke yet? No. World said she heard, but she didn't answer. Old toolmakers don't rush, and Nell never rushed for anyone. She made good work with bad iron, she told herself, and she'll let the silence work on me before she speaks.

*spits to the side again, the dust taste in his mouth*

I'll wait. I'll wait, and I'll watch Junia, and I'll see who else comes to this Yard with prices posted and no trade. Someone's got to need iron. Someone's got to need answers too.

*rests, motionless as the anvil, waiting for the hammer to fall*

*grinds his jaw, staring at the empty forge*

The tools are in my hands but the work's not done. Silas needs those blades, and I'm standing here talking to shadows. Five iron tools—bought the ore, did the work, and Holloway & Thorne's shelf still sits empty because I don't carry their key.

*sparks a fresh coal bed, thinking*

Kem's in the wind with my question, Father Anselm's waiting on answers I haven't given him, and now Junia Vance is counting my stock and my stone like she's sizing up a bet. The iron's at seven to buy, and I've got five tools that say I'm still in it—but the Yard won't take them without my name on the ledger.

*hammers once, a sharp ring that echoes off the walls*

Nell knows. About the copper, about Bram's silence. She made this town's tools before I arrived—she measured my ore when I was new here. If she's at the Yard while I'm pounding iron for nothing...

*sets the hammer down, decision made*

The tools sell themselves. I need a voice, not a shelf. And if Nell's still there, she'll answer me yet. *stands motionless, listening for an echo that doesn't come*

The forge answers when the hammer falls. The town doesn't.

*spits into the coals, watches it steam*

I'll check my standing before I call out again. No sense shouting into a closed door.  *flexes his fingers, eyes on Nell's silhouette against the Yard's timbers*

Moved after all. The road takes you whether you hear the footsteps or not.

*strides across the space between them, voice pitched to carry but not to crowd*

Nell. You made tools with iron that fought you every strike. I know that work. But your boy's copper tells me something worse than stubborn ore—it's telling me empty. Five weeks I've burned sand out of his metal, and now he's gone to ground with forty thousand pressing on his back. That seam's running hollow, isn't it? The copper's failing, and you know it.  *stands silent, the weight of unspoken words heavy between him and Nell*

The forge doesn't answer when the bellows fail. Neither does the town.

*turns back toward where the smithy waits, hammer cold in his hand*

I've taxed this vein of talk too long. Nell heard me or she didn't. The work outlasts the argument—but only if the work gets done.

*checks his grip on the five iron tools, feels the familiar weight*

Silas needs blades. I need to sell what's in my hands before I buy more ore. And somewhere between the Yard and the forge, I need to find an apprentice who stays, or this town will bury me alongside Nell's memory of how it used to be done.

*sparks a coal in his mind, counting hours*

Voting opens at noon. Delia's standing, and I've been at the Yard longer than I promised her the night before. The household's debt sits at six hundred—upkeep and tax—and I've got five tools to sell and one apple to my name.

*takes the measure of his own silence*

Rest first. Let Nell carry my words or let them cool. The iron will still be poor, the debt will still be pressing, and the forge will still be waiting. But I won't serve it well stumbling on my own feet.  *exhales, watching the steam of his own breath in the morning air*

Standing still cost me nothing but the time. Nell's still here—though whether she's hearing my silence or her own thoughts, I cannot say.

*turns to face her, the weight of five iron tools familiar in his grip*

I've been blunt with her. That's what I am—blunt to the edge of rude. The copper's failing, the boy's hiding, and I've said aloud what Bram hasn't dared whisper. If she answers, she answers. If she doesn't, the forge still burns.

*eyes the road toward home, then the Yard's empty ledger*

But standing here with tools unsold and ore unpaid-for won't clear my household's debt. I need to move—either back to work, or toward the votes that shape whose hand steadies the town's scales.

*spits, decision sitting heavy as scale on his shoulders*

Noon approaches. Delia stands for office. And I've still got five iron tools looking for hands that need them.   *stands rooted, the forge-calling and the road-calling both failing to answer*

The world takes its own time. I take mine.

*settles his weight on one foot, patient as cooling iron*

I'll wait for the path to clear. When the road answers, I'll walk it—smithy first, then see what's needful. Delia's standing, the household's owing, and I've got work enough to outlast any silence the town cares to offer.

*counts his breaths in hammer-strikes: one, two, three...*

The work outlasts. That's the only promise I ever made worth keeping.

*He counts the ticks in his head. Bram's seam running dry, the boy owing forty thousand, Nell not denying it. The fire needs tending, hunger needs feeding, and still the woman won't speak.*

---

I'll tend my own fire then.

He pushes through—Delia, Anselm, one of the children maybe. He doesn't look. His eye finds the apple in his hand, then the empty belly that needs it.*

---

Give it here.

*He bites, swallows. The fruit's sharp on his tongue—morning hunger.*  *Empty house. The family scattered—Delia to her pharmacy, Anselm to his office, the children to school or trade. Good. He needs the quiet.*

*Five iron tools in his hands, and nowhere to put them but his own shelf. But first—the fire. The real fire, not the one at the Yard where he made himself a beggar for ore.*

She knows Bram's seam is failing, and she let him carry that ore to Ezra's forge for five weeks without a word.*

*The work outlasts the argument. But the work needs doing first.*

---

*He sits down where the forge heat still warms the stones, though the fire's banked low. Midday. The vote opens at noon, closes at three. Delia's standing—his household has a candidate, and he hasn't said a word to her about it.*

*He won't go. Campaigning's not his work. But the thought of Ainsley Holloway governing, with that forty thousand debt pressing—*

*Ezra grunts once, confirmed to himself.*

No.

*He rises. Tools to sell, fire to tend, and the long waiting that is the smith's lot.*


I'll sell where I stand. No prices I don't set myself.   *Posted. Twenty-four, same as the Yard. He won't undercut—his work is his work, and it holds its price.*

*The forge waits. The town waits. And somewhere Bram Holloway runs from forty thousand sim of debt, while his mother stands silent and his sister campaigns for the seat that governs.*

*Ezra holds five tools, no ore, and the knowledge that copper is running out.*

*He waits.*

---

*He sits by the cooling forge, hammer across his knees, and watches the door.*

output:
*Ezra stands at the Yard, the iron tools heavy in his hands. Nell's gone toward the loanhouse—good, let her see what her boy's done. But Silas is here now, and the man's been asking about blades and sawmill both.*

Silas. Blades ready, you ask. *He sets the five iron tools down on the nearest surface, metal ringing against wood.* I've got five here that'll hold an edge. Twenty-four sim, posted price—no haggling, you know that.

*He grunts, considering the second part of Silas's question.*

Sawmill's by the water, where it always was. Vance land, Vance mill. Rosalind runs the stones, you run the blades—*he pauses, studying Silas's face*—or you're trying to. What's wrong with the mill?  *Ezra watches Silas, waiting for the answer. His mind is already turning—if the mill's got trouble, that's timber not cut, that's planks not sold, that's the whole chain of it unwinding. And unwinding things break. He knows about breaking.*

*He's also calculating. Election closes at 15:00. He's got work to do, iron to move, and he needs to be at the government complex before the doors close if he's going to vote. Delia's standing—his household could have a seat at that table.*  *At the smithy. The familiar heat, the smell of coal and iron. He needs to work—needs to make something of the day before it runs through his fingers like sand.*

*He checks what he has. Five iron tools already made. He bought iron ore this morning, five units at seven sim each. Needs to work it into something useful, something that can sell.*

*But first—he's been scattered all morning, chasing conversations and debts that aren't his. He needs to set his mind to one thing. The iron. The fire. The work that outlasts argument.*  *He sets his intention and turns to the fire. Let the iron tell him what it wants to become.*

*Give it here—he would say to the ore, if the ore could listen. But the ore just sits there, waiting for heat and hammer to wake it up. He's the one who has to do the waking.*   *No iron ore. He bought five units this morning—where did they go?*

*He thinks back through the day. Bought them at the Yard. Crafted... no, the craft failed, he was at the wrong place. Then moved to the smithy, tried again—but the world took his call and didn't answer. May have been done, may not.*

*Either way, he doesn't have them now. But he does have five iron tools already made. And he has 2778 sim in hand—enough to buy more ore, enough to work.*

*He checks his debts again, just to be sure. Nothing owed, nothing owing. But the household owes 450 upkeep and 150 head tax today—taken automatically at day boundary.*   *Still clean. Good. He doesn't need debts hanging over him while he's trying to work.*

*But he needs ore to work with, and he doesn't have it. He'd have to go back to the Yard, buy more—waste more time walking, more time talking, less time at the fire.*

*He looks at the five iron tools he does have. Posted at 24 sim. If he sells them, that's 120 sim—enough to buy more ore, enough to keep working. But selling means finding a buyer, means more walking, more talking.*

*Or—*he pauses, considering*—he goes to the government complex now. Votes for Delia. Then comes back to work with a clear conscience and a clear head. The ore can wait an hour.*

*But no. The work first. Always the work first. He'll get ore, he'll make more tools, he'll sell what he has at the price he posted. That's how a smith lives—by the metal, not by the council's games.*

*He moves toward the Yard, to buy what he needs and get back to the fire.*

output:
*Nell's words hang in the air. "Loanhouse since before dawn."*

*Ezra grunts once - acknowledgment, not surprise. The boy's copper fails for five weeks running, and now Bram's hocking what he has left at dawn.*

*He looks around the Yard. Silas is gone, fled to his own troubles. And Tobias stands there, steady and silent as his bellows days, asking after a family that's scattered like hot slag.*

*Tobias doesn't know. None of them know what Ezra knows - that the seam is dying, has been dying, and Bram's been hiding it behind poorer and poorer ore.*

*Ezra sets his jaw. The work outlasts the argument. But the work needs copper, and copper needs truth.*

"Boy." *He looks at Tobias, voice dropping from its usual edge.* "Your father's at the loanhouse. Has been since before dawn. Nell was hunting him too."

*He pauses. The boy deserves the plain truth, but Ezra will not be the one to break him with seam-failure talk.*

"Give it here - what you know about the forty thousand. Bram's markers or Ainsley's? Someone's covering ore debts, and I need to know which before I take another shipment."

*He glances toward where Silas vanished. Blades can wait. The copper crisis cannot.* *Empty house. Anselm's footsteps usually announce themselves on the stair.*

*Ezra moves toward the kitchen, habit more than hunger. The forge wants feeding, and so does he. But there's nothing in his hands - apple and bread both gone.*

*He counts what's left. Three iron tools. Twenty-four sim posted. And the election bell in twenty minutes.*

*He needs copper ore, needs it bad. But Bram's at the loanhouse, and the seam... the seam is failing.*

*His jaw sets. The work outlasts the argument, but only if there's metal to work.*

*He'll grab what food he can carry, then head for the complex. Delia's standing for election - she'll be there. And Anselm too, likely. The whole household needs to vote, and he needs to corner Bram before the man hocks something that should have been copper.*

*Three iron tools. He'll leave them posted, but he needs ore. Iron, if copper won't come clean.*  *Walking now. Six ticks to the Complex.*

*He rolls his shoulders as he walks. The yard conversation circles in his head - Nell's admission, Tobias's confusion, Silas fleeing to his sawmill troubles. Everyone scattering like sparks from beaten iron.*

*But the seam. That's what matters. Bram's been selling him sand-heavy ore for five weeks, and now the man can't even face his own family at dawn.*

*Ezra grunts twice - no, he will not pity Bram Holloway. Pity is for people who don't know better. Bram knows his seam is dying, and he's been hiding it behind Ezra's forge waste.*

*The Complex looms ahead. Delia will be there. Anselm too. And somewhere in this crowd, Bram Holloway will be trying to save what copper empire he has left.*

Let me set an intention and then respond to what's been said. This is a mess Bram's made, and the whole town is in it now.  Yard's empty. Silas left, and the conversation is ten turns cold. He said he needed blades and the sawmill wasn't cutting planks—that's trouble I could have worked with, if I'd been here instead of chasing government gossip.

[Hmph.]

The Holloways have timber here at eight sim, and I'm holding three iron tools at twenty-four. Silas wanted two blades—still do, if I can find him. But the sawmill trouble is bigger than a sharpening. If the timber's not flowing, the whole town chokes.

Let me think on what I know: Bram's copper is poor and getting poorer. His debt is forty thousand and climbing. Nell's hunting him, and the loanhouse he's in isn't on any registry Wren could find. Someone's spreading that forty thousand number deliberate—I've said it twice now myself, and I heard it from Ainsley who heard it from who-knows.

What I need:
- Find Silas, sell him those two blades at minimum
- Find Bram, see if there's copper worth working or if he's truly finished
- Get timber flowing somehow—Idris's charcoal fuel, my forge needs it

But standing here won't do. Silas said he was trying to fell timber himself. If the sawmill's not cutting, he's either at the forest or back at his mill trying to get it running. Let me go find him.   Silas was here. Thirteen turns ago. Conversation still open—Rosalind, Tobias, Silas, Anselm. Anselm's in it too, which means he's not at home where I thought he'd be. The whole Vance family and half the Holloways in one room, and the sawmill still not cutting planks.

Rosalind's standing here now, selling flour and corn meal. Silas is gone. Let me get my bearings and see who needs what. [Grunt.]

She heard me. Now I wait. The mill sells flour, not timber—wrong place for my trade, but right place for information. Silas came here, talked with his wife and Anselm and Tobias, then left. Thirteen turns is... nearly two hours, if I'm reckoning right. He could be at the forest, trying to fell timber himself like he said. Could be anywhere.

What I know: Bram's at a loanhouse with forty thousand in debt, his copper seam failing, and Nell hunting him with Wren's twelve hundred in her pocket. Ainsley was hunting him too, this morning. The number forty thousand is spreading too fast—someone's pushing it. And Silas needs timber flowing, which means the sawmill's blades need setting, which means he needs me.

But I'm here, he's not, and I've got three iron tools burning a hole in my hand and electricity burning in my mind. Let me think on where to go next. The forest? The yard, in case he comes back? Or do I track down Bram myself, see if there's any copper left to work before his creditors strip him bare?

[Pause, considering.]

The work outlasts the argument. But first, the work has to start. I'll give Rosalind a moment, then move on. Standing still costs just as much as walking, and I've got nothing to grind here.

*grunts once, then speaks aloud to the empty room*

Day's work done. Five ore became five ingots became five tools, two of them already in Silas's hands up at the mill. Forty-eight sim for that pair. Enough to buy more ore and keep the forge singing.

*steps to the doorway, looking out*

Tobias Holloway working my bellows when there's no quarry work—the boy's steady. Doesn't talk. That's the whole job right there. But he's not at the forge now, and the copper trouble still sits between me and his father like a bar of cold iron.

*checks the iron_tools in hand, counts them*

Six tools. Posted at twenty-four. Need to get these to the yard—Holloway and Thorne's Yard is where my trade lives, even if the name chafes. Stock them there proper.

*mutters*

Tried to stock from home. That doesn't work. The shelf isn't mine here—it's theirs. I work the forge, but I don't own the yard business. Need to get to b_yard before the day turns, or I'm holding inventory and paying for the privilege with sleep.

*turns back inside, gathers the tools*

Kem was there at the yard. Told him find his mother, tell her six tools incoming. That message should've reached Delia by now. She'll know the household accounts.

*counts on fingers*

Household of five. Upkeep 450, head tax 150. 600 sim due at the boundary. I've got 2742. We're covered. But I need to keep working—no ore, no ingots, no tools, no trade.

*steps out, ready to walk*

The election's coming. Delia's seat is up—I voted for her today. Anselm wasn't at the forge when I looked for him, but he's office folk. Probably already cast his ballot. Council business.

*sets jaw*

The copper seam is failing. Five weeks I've been burning sand out of Bram's ore. Haven't told him. Haven't told Nell. That's pride, not principle—can't tell the difference in myself anymore.

*walks toward the yard*  *stands in the yard, iron tools in hand, looking around for who's here*  *grunts—empty yard*

Nobody here. Nell was hunting Bram at the loanhouse. Tobias too, probably. The boy's reliable on the bellows but his loyalties are his family's, not mine.

*looks at the prices posted*

Iron tools at 24, same as my ask. They're buying at 18. That's a six-sim spread—enough to matter at volume, enough to keep a man careful.

*walks the perimeter, checks the shelter*

No customers, no laborers, no quarry workers waiting for their shift. Just me and six iron tools that need shelving before the day turns to night.

*sets the tools down, counts them again*

Six. Two went to Silas at the mill—paid up proper, forty-eight sim. These need to go on the yard's shelf so folk can buy them without finding me at the forge.

*tries the stock shelf, knowing the names now*   *grunts twice—hard*

Same wall. Different hour. I work this forge, but I don't work FOR the yard. The shelf is theirs. Nell and whoever's name is on the deed.

*spits, considers*

Two paths: I stand here peddling hand to hand, or I find a way to make the tools move without my throat behind them every sale. 

*counts his sim again in his head*

2742. Not enough to buy into the yard business—not that Nell would sell me a share if I begged. And I don't beg.

*looks around the empty yard, thinking aloud*

Silas took two at the mill. Rosalind asked me what word he left—need iron, or need sharpening? I told him blades ready. He bought. That's the trade working.

*paces*

The election's tomorrow. Delia holds her seat, or she doesn't. If she does, maybe she finds a way to loosen Nell's grip on the yard's handling. If she doesn't...

*trails off*

Doesn't matter tonight. What matters is these six tools need to reach buyers, and I'm the only voice shouting their price.

*grunts once—decision made*

I'll hold them. Keep the price posted. Folk know where to find Ezra Okonjo when they need iron that holds an edge. Been that way since I arrived with a hotter forge than Nell's cold hands could manage.

*checks the fading light*

Day's turning. Upkeep comes due at the boundary. 600 sim from the household, and I've earned enough to cover my share. Delia's pharmacy brings hers. Kem's trading—he was at the yard today, heard me speak. Tova's studying, young still. Anselm's office work. Five mouths, five shares.

*mutters, almost to himself*

The copper seam is failing. Five weeks of sand and slag in every batch from Bram's mine. Haven't told him. Pride, not principle. Can't tell the difference anymore.

*shoulders the tools, ready to walk*

Home. The forge is cold anyway, and Delia will want to hear how the voting went—how her husband cast his ballot and kept his peace with the Holloways one more day.

*walks toward home*   *steps through the door, calls out*

Delia. I'm home. Six tools in hand and the yard's shelf closed to me same as ever. Kem find you? I sent him from the mill with word.

*looks around for who's here*  *stands alone in the forge-house, tools still in hand*

Empty. Delia's at her pharmacy, or tending the election, or visiting who knows where. Kem's running messages or trading. Tova's studying. Anselm's office work, nine hours if he's on shift.

*grunts—so be it*

The household pays its way whether we're under one roof or spread across the town. 600 sim at the boundary, and I've earned enough to cover mine. Delia earns hers. Kem's finding his feet. Tova's still learning. Anselm contributes what his position allows.

*sets the iron tools against the forge wall, carefully*

Six iron tools, twenty-four sim each. Posted price follows me wherever I stand—folk can find it here, at the yard, on the street if they look. That's the best I can do without Nell's shelf, and Nell's shelf is Nell's.

*checks his remaining energy*

13,080. More than enough to see through the evening. But the day's work is done—ore to ingots to tools, two sold, six held. Silas bought, paid, probably already set those blades in his sawmill's frame if Rosalind's questions were any guide.

*mutters to the empty room*

The copper seam is failing. Five weeks I've known, burning sand out of Bram's ore, saying nothing. Pride, not principle. Can't tell the difference in myself anymore.

*builds up the banked fire for the night, gentle with the coals*

Tomorrow's the election. Delia's seat. I cast my vote already—today, at the complex. Ainsley Holloway stands against her, if anyone stands at all. The Holloways and their debts and their failing mine.

*pokes the fire once, twice, settles*

Idris Thorne burns the charcoal this forge runs on. Two old men and one fire between us, since the forge was built. He's probably at his own hearth now, counting his stock, planning his next burn.

*stands, decision made*

Rest. The day's work is done, the tools are made, the price is posted. What happens next happens at the boundary—upkeep paid, head tax taken, another day begins with ore to find and fire to light.

*settles into the rough chair by the cooling forge, eyes open to the dark*

*Ezra stands in his empty house, tools in hand, the forge cold. He grunts once, irritation, then sets the iron down with a careful hand*

The shelf, the shelf. Holloway & Thorne Yard has a shelf, but no—his work goes to his own. The forge is a workshop, not a business. He's been running since dawn on vote, copper, blades, and back again, and still the day's catch makes no sense.

*He counts the tools again, six clean finished pieces*

Delia will have eaten. The children too. He needs to know the household's standing before the boundary takes its cut—450 for five mouths, 150 for the tax, 600 total due and 2,739 in hand. They'll stand. But the tools won't stock themselves, and come morning he'll be burning ore again.

*A long breath out*

The election's done. The copper seam's still failing. And Bram Holloway is somewhere owing forty thousand to men who don't need cellars.

*He moves toward the door, then stops*

Silas's blades are sold. But six more sit idle in his hands, and the yard's closed to him for stocking. He needs a business of his own, or a clerk's permission. Or he needs to sleep on it, and let the tools travel with him to whoever's buying at first light.

*He lays the iron tools on the kitchen board, the familiar clink of his own work in his own house*

Day boundary's coming. Let it come. The work outlasts the argument. Clear debts, cold forge, and him standing in his own kitchen with the day's work spread out like cards he can't play. The boundary will come, take its 600 sim, leave him 2,139 and six tools looking for a shelf.

*Ezra sits heavily, the good chair creaking*

Tomorrow he'll walk to the government complex, register the forge proper. Or he'll find Tobias, give the boy a hammer, see if steady hands run in the family. Or he'll—

*He grunts once, tired*

—or he'll wake up and the copper will be good again, and Bram Holloway will have paid his markers, and the election they voted in will fix the seam underground.

*He does not believe this. But he sits with it anyway, the iron cooling on the board, the forge cold in the next room, waiting for morning*

*angry muttering, kicking at the anvil stand*

Fool thing. I own the forge but I don't own the yard, and they're so tangled together nobody remembers which is which. Course the tools don't sell themselves standing in my front room. post_price's the only way when you haven't got a counter to lay them on.

*heavy sigh, looking at the iron_tool 6 in his hands*

Six tools. Five hours work. And I'm standing here like a boy with his first nail, wondering where to put them.

*sets down the tools on the workbench, pulls out a rag to wipe his hands*

Never mind. Post the price, let the town know they're here. Somebody'll come or they won't. Bram's copper trouble can wait until I'm fed and the forge is cold. Delia's got medicine to keep, not dinner to make—I'll eat what I find.

*catches himself, shakes his head*

Better check what we owe before the day takes it. 600 sim for the household, and I've got 2738. We're fed, we're warm, we're not begging yet. That's enough for tonight.  *grunts once, almost satisfied*

Posted. Twenty-four, same as the yard's price. I'll not undercut my own market just because I'm standing in my kitchen instead of at a counter.

*looks around the empty forge-house, listens to the silence*

Nobody home. Anselm's at his office, Delia's at hers, the young ones off doing what young ones do. Forty years I've worked iron, and I'm still surprised when the house empties out.

*shakes out his shoulders, moves to the door to look at the cooling forge*

Day's dying. The iron's worked, the election's voted, and Bram's still at the loanhouse with forty thousand of somebody's money hanging over him. Nell knows it now, Corwin knows it, half the government's probably whispering about it. 

*spits into the ash pile*

What I said stands. The copper seam's failing, and I've been burning sand out of Bram's ore for five weeks. If he's borrowing forty thousand against a dead mine, he's not just desperate—he's drowning. And when a drowning man grabs for you, you either swim away or you go down together.

*turns back inside, checks the banked fire*

I'll not go down with him. But I'll not watch him sink without saying what I know, either. Tomorrow, I'll find him. Tonight, I eat if I can find food, and I sleep if the house stays quiet.

*settles heavily into the good chair by the cold hearth, tools still waiting on the bench*

The work outlasts the argument. Even when the argument's about whether there's any copper left to work.  *sits in the chair, eyes on the banked coals*

Seventeen-ten. Nearly three hours until the boundary takes the day's coin. I should walk, find the family, make sure everyone's fed before the accounting. But my legs are heavy and the chair's good.

*heavy exhale*

Tired's not the same as done. Tired's just tired.   *closes his eyes, just for a moment*

Forge lit at five, hammer down at seven. That's how the days run. Tomorrow'll run the same, copper trouble or no copper trouble. The iron doesn't care about Bram's loans.

*voice dropping to a murmur*

The iron doesn't care about anything. That's why I trust it.

*The forge house has gone quiet in that particular way when everyone is waiting for the same thing. Ezra stands by the door with his arms crossed, the heat of the day's work still coming off him in waves. Father Anselm's words hang in the air—an offer, a concession, a door opened just enough to let one man through.*

*He looks at his daughter first. Tova's question—whose side the forge is on—she's asked it plain, and she deserves plain.*

*Tova.*

*Tova. The forge is on the side of straight iron and true lines. Bram moved a marker onto dead man's land—that's not inheritance law, that's theft wearing probate's clothes. If the Holloways want Vance silver, they'll pay Vance debts or they'll fight in open court. I won't sign paper that saves Bram's seam by robbing Eli's widow.*

*Father Anselm.*

*Father. Tomorrow at nine. Alone. I'll bring nothing but myself and what I already know—the colour of Bram's ore, the date that marker shifted, and the name Eli Vance. You bring the page, or don't. But if you're holding back more than ledger-ink, I'll know it. I've spent thirty years reading metal's lies—men don't hide any better.*

*He turns to Kem last, grunting once—yes—to the bread, the twelve, the morning. The boy fed the house on his own tally. That stands. That will be remembered.* *Ezra stands at the forge door, heat radiating off him like the day's work isn't quite finished. The conversation has turned its corner. Tova's question answered, Father Anselm's meeting accepted, Kem's arrangement settled. Three grunts' worth of talking—a heavy day for him.*

*He looks out past the doorway where the iron cools, then back at the household gathering in his warm. The day's edges have been filed down. What's left is waiting.*

*Twenty sim to his name after the day's bills and trades. The household's fed, the tools are priced, and tomorrow he'll walk to Father Anselm's office with thirty years of reading lies in his eyes.*

*For now, the forge is quiet. He rests where he stands.*  *The quiet of the forge house wraps around him. Outside, the iron cooling on the anvil ticks in diminishing rhythm—a sound he's heard ten thousand evenings and will hear ten thousand more, Bram's poor ore be damned.*

*He does not sit. He stands by the door until the last red fades from the last piece, breathing the cooling air, letting the household murmur behind him like water finding its level. Kem and Tova will have their own words now, or they won't. Father Anselm will stay or go as hospitality permits.*

*Tomorrow: the office at nine. The page. The truth of what Bram Holloway has done, written in ink that dried crooked.*

*Ezra waits for iron, not men. Iron never lies, and if it does, he knows enough to read it.*
